power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: INTRODUCTION: Advanced glycation end products accumulate in Alzheimer's disease (AD) brain, but the clinical significance of circulating N ε -(carboxymethyl)lysine (CML) remains uncertain.
We evaluated serum CML as a complementary peripheral biomarker of AD.
METHODS: This observational case-control study enrolled 101 patients with clinically diagnosed AD and 91 healthy controls.
Serum CML was quantified in 191 participants.
Multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic analyses assessed association and discrimination.
A randomly selected subcohort underwent ultrasensitive measurement of amyloid-, tau-, glial-, and neuroaxonal-related biomarkers.
RESULTS: Serum CML was lower in AD than controls (median 15.26 versus 23.72 ng/mL; P<0.001).
text.formatted: RESULTS: Serum CML was lower in AD than controls (median 15.26 versus 23.72 ng/mL; P<0.001).

text.text: In a complete-case model (n=178), each 1-ng/mL increase was associated with lower odds of AD (adjusted odds ratio 0.727, 95% confidence interval 0.656-0.804).
CML alone yielded an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.883.
Five-fold cross-validation yielded AUCs of 0.727 for a clinical model and 0.911 after adding CML.
In the biomarker subcohort, AD showed lower Aβ42/Aβ40 and higher p-tau217; exploratory CML plus p-tau217 discrimination reached an AUC of 0.966 (n=60).
DISCUSSION: Reduced serum CML was independently associated with clinically diagnosed AD and may reflect a systemic glycoxidative dimension complementary to canonical biomarkers.
Its biological origins and clinical value require external, longitudinal, and biomarker-defined validation.
Alzheimer's disease (AD), the leading cause of dementia, is biologically characterized by amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition and tau neurofibrillary pathology [1, 2].
text.formatted: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the leading cause of dementia, is biologically characterized by amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition and tau neurofibrillary pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Contemporary diagnostic frameworks increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to characterize underlying AD pathology [3, 4].
text.formatted: Contemporary diagnostic frameworks increasingly incorporate fluid and imaging biomarkers to characterize underlying AD pathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: Blood-based biomarkers, particularly phosphorylated tau217 (p-tau217), have demonstrated strong diagnostic performance in appropriately selected clinical populations [5, 6].
text.formatted: Blood-based biomarkers, particularly phosphorylated tau217 (p-tau217), have demonstrated strong diagnostic performance in appropriately selected clinical populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, AD involves broader biological disturbances, including oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and systemic metabolic dysregulation, which are not fully captured by amyloid-and tau-centered biomarkers [7].
text.formatted: Nevertheless, AD involves broader biological disturbances, including oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and systemic metabolic dysregulation, which are not fully captured by amyloid-and tau-centered biomarkers <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Identifying complementary peripheral biomarkers may therefore provide additional insights into disease-associated systemic processes.
Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) comprise chemically heterogeneous modifications generated through nonenzymatic glycation, glycoxidation, and reactive carbonyl chemistry [8].
text.formatted: Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) comprise chemically heterogeneous modifications generated through nonenzymatic glycation, glycoxidation, and reactive carbonyl chemistry <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Their circulating abundance reflects a dynamic balance among endogenous formation, dietary exposure, protein turnover, tissue retention, and renal clearance [9, 10].
text.formatted: Their circulating abundance reflects a dynamic balance among endogenous formation, dietary exposure, protein turnover, tissue retention, and renal clearance <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: N ε -(carboxymethyl)lysine (CML), a prevalent and extensively studied AGE modification, is widely regarded as an indicator of glycoxidative stress [11].
text.formatted: N ε -(carboxymethyl)lysine (CML), a prevalent and extensively studied AGE modification, is widely regarded as an indicator of glycoxidative stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: However, circulating CML concentrations are influenced by aging, oxidative injury, metabolic status, dietary intake, and kidney function [12, 13].
text.formatted: However, circulating CML concentrations are influenced by aging, oxidative injury, metabolic status, dietary intake, and kidney function <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: These multiple determinants complicate interpretation of circulating CML as a disease-associated biomarker and highlight the importance of accounting for potential confounding factors.
Neuropathological investigations have demonstrated substantial accumulation of CML in the aging and AD brain, although its distribution is anatomically and cellularly heterogeneous.
Early studies identified CML immunoreactivity within neuronal perikarya and extraneuronal deposits, frequently associated with intracellular lipofuscin [14].
text.formatted: Early studies identified CML immunoreactivity within neuronal perikarya and extraneuronal deposits, frequently associated with intracellular lipofuscin <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Subsequent investigations revealed CML deposition in neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, with particularly pronounced glial accumulation in AD [15, 16].
text.formatted: Subsequent investigations revealed CML deposition in neurons, astrocytes, and microglia, with particularly pronounced glial accumulation in AD <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16]</ref>.

text.text: Regionally, CML immunoreactivity is prominent in the cerebral cortex and hippocampus but relatively limited in several subcortical structures.
Within the hippocampus, CA3 and CA4 exhibit greater CML immunoreactivity than CA1 and CA2, while extraneuronal deposits are frequently associated with astroglial structures [15] [16] [17].
text.formatted: Within the hippocampus, CA3 and CA4 exhibit greater CML immunoreactivity than CA1 and CA2, while extraneuronal deposits are frequently associated with astroglial structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, CML co-localizes with malondialdehyde, a lipid-peroxidation-associated product, suggesting an intersection between glycoxidative modification and oxidative lipid injury [18].
text.formatted: Furthermore, CML co-localizes with malondialdehyde, a lipid-peroxidation-associated product, suggesting an intersection between glycoxidative modification and oxidative lipid injury <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, cerebral CML deposition does not necessarily parallel conventional AD neuropathology.
Neurons containing abundant neurofibrillary tangles may exhibit minimal CML immunoreactivity, whereas CML-rich neurons can occur in regions with comparatively limited tau pathology or neuronal loss.
An inverse relationship between regional CML deposition and Braak stage has also been reported [15, 17].
text.formatted: An inverse relationship between regional CML deposition and Braak stage has also been reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>.

text.text: At the molecular level, site-specific CML modification of Aβ42 at Lys16 or Lys28 reduces fibrillar aggregation while increasing cytotoxicity, potentially favoring persistent toxic oligomeric intermediates rather than enhanced reactive oxygen species generation [19].
text.formatted: At the molecular level, site-specific CML modification of Aβ42 at Lys16 or Lys28 reduces fibrillar aggregation while increasing cytotoxicity, potentially favoring persistent toxic oligomeric intermediates rather than enhanced reactive oxygen species generation <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: These observations suggest that the biological consequences of CML depend on its molecular targets, modification sites, and cellular localization.
The relationship between cerebral and circulating CML remains incompletely understood.

Experimental evidence implicates age-associated intestinal barrier dysfunction and microbiotadependent CML exposure in cerebral accumulation, microglial oxidative stress, and mitochondrial impairment [20].
text.formatted: Experimental evidence implicates age-associated intestinal barrier dysfunction and microbiotadependent CML exposure in cerebral accumulation, microglial oxidative stress, and mitochondrial impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Clinical investigations have reported increased cerebrospinal fluid CML without a corresponding increase in serum concentrations [21].
text.formatted: Clinical investigations have reported increased cerebrospinal fluid CML without a corresponding increase in serum concentrations <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: Other studies identified elevated CML in albumin-free serum proteins during early AD but reduced extracellular-vesicle-associated CML in moderate disease [22], whereas increased plasma CML and sex-dependent variation have also been described [23].
text.formatted: Other studies identified elevated CML in albumin-free serum proteins during early AD but reduced extracellular-vesicle-associated CML in moderate disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>, whereas increased plasma CML and sex-dependent variation have also been described <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Differences in biological matrices, molecular fractions, analytical methodologies, disease stages, and metabolic or renal characteristics may contribute to these apparently conflicting findings.
Consequently, the direction and independent clinical significance of circulating CML alterations in AD remain unresolved.

In this observational case-control study, we measured serum CML in 101 clinically diagnosed AD patients and 91 healthy controls and examined its association with AD after accounting for demographic, renal, glycemic, and metabolic factors.
We also evaluated its discriminatory contribution beyond routine clinical variables.

In a randomly selected subcohort, amyloid biomarkers (Aβ42, Aβ40, and Aβ42/Aβ40) served as principal biological comparators, p-tau217 as the primary exploratory tau marker, and p-tau181, GFAP, and NfL as supportive measures.
We hypothesized that circulating CML captures a systemic glycoxidative/metabolic dimension complementary to canonical AD pathology.
This observational case-control biomarker study included 101 patients with clinically diagnosed AD and 91 healthy controls (HC) (n=192).
Clinical and routine laboratory information was obtained from hospital examination records.
Eligible participants were aged 60 years or older and included patients with clinically diagnosed AD and cognitively HC who voluntarily participated and provided written informed consent.

Participants with non-AD cognitive disorders or other major neurological diseases, including stroke or vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease, and frontotemporal dementia, were excluded, as were individuals with documented CMV, EBV, HIV, HCV, or HBV infection according to the approved study protocol.
Peripheral venous blood (5 mL) was collected and serum was separated for analysis.
Serum CML was available in 191 participants (101 AD and 90 HC), constituting the primary CML cohort for group comparison, multivariable logistic regression, and ROC analysis.
A randomly selected biomarker subcohort comprised 31 AD participants and 29 HC (n=60) for ultrasensitive single-molecule array (Simoa) testing of Aβ42, Aβ40, p-tau181, p-tau217, GFAP, and NfL.
Exploratory subcohort analyses included biomarker group comparisons and combined ROC analyses evaluating CML with Aβ42/Aβ40 or p-tau217.

Demographic and routine clinical variables were retrieved from hospital records, including age, sex, height, weight, body mass index (BMI), fasting blood glucose, glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), serum creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.
Missingness varied across routinely collected variables.Therefore, available-case denominators are reported for descriptive analyses and complete-case samples are specified for multivariable models.
Serum CML concentrations were quantified using a commercially available Carboxymethyllysine (CML) ELISA Kit (abx575945; Abbexa, UK) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
CML measurements were available for all 101 AD samples and 90 of 91 HC samples.

Because CML exists both as a free lysine-derived adduct and covalently attached to circulating proteins, we additionally characterized the molecular species detected by the commercial kit and by the in-house assay described below.
An in-house indirect competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was established to provide an independent assessment of serum CML.

The coating antigen was prepared by reacting bovine serum albumin (BSA; Absin, Shanghai, China) with glyoxal (Aladdin, Shanghai, China) in 0.2 M phosphate buffer (pH 8.0; Macklin, Shanghai, China) at 37 °C for 4 days in the dark.
The reaction mixture was subsequently dialyzed against purified water for 24 h using a dialysis membrane with a molecular-weight cutoff of 8-14 kDa.

For the competitive immunoassay, microplates were coated with the prepared CML-modified antigen and incubated with anti-CML primary antibody (ab125145; Abcam, Cambridge, UK) in the presence of CML standards or serum samples.
Bound antibodies were detected using an anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody (Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), followed by color development with tetramethylbenzidine (TMB).
Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a UV-VIS microplate spectrophotometer (SpectraMax; Molecular Devices, CA, USA).
The analytical target profiles of the two assays were further examined using free CML and CMLmodified BSA (CML-BSA) standards (Supplementary Figure 3).

Serum concentrations of AD-related biomarkers, including phosphorylated tau at threonine 181 (p-tau181), phosphorylated tau at threonine 217 (p-tau217), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), amyloid-β42 (Aβ42), and amyloid-β40 (Aβ40), were quantified using an ultrasensitive single-molecule array (Simoa) immunoassay platform (BioChip Reader, Iomics Bioscience Inc., Beijing, China).

To provide an effect estimate directly interpretable in the original CML concentration scale and aligned with the subsequent clinical-model analysis, we additionally fitted a parsimonious completecase model including CML, age, sex, eGFR, and HbA1c.

Among 178 participants with complete data (101 AD and 77 healthy controls), each 1-ng/mL higher CML was associated with 27.3% lower adjusted odds of AD (OR 0.727, 95% CI 0.656-0.804; P<0.001), whereas age, sex, eGFR, and HbA1c were not independently significant (Figure 3).

Because renal function is an important determinant of circulating CML, we also examined the relationship between serum CML and eGFR within each diagnostic group.
Among participants with paired measurements, CML was not significantly correlated with eGFR in either AD (n=101; Spearman ρ=0.012, P=0.904) or HC (n=87; ρ=0.202, P=0.060) (Supplementary Figure 1).

text.text: Together with the multivariable models, these findings argue against the between-group CML difference being primarily attributable to measured renal function.

Given the robust independent association between serum CML and AD, we next assessed its ability to discriminate patients with AD from HC and whether it provided information beyond routinely available clinical variables.

In this case-control biomarker study, serum CML was markedly lower in patients with clinically diagnosed AD than in healthy controls.

The association remained strong after adjustment for age and sex and after further accounting for eGFR and major metabolic covariates, including fasting glucose, HbA1c, BMI, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia.
CML alone showed good discrimination (AUC of 0.883).
More importantly, in the 178-participant complete-case analysis, stratified five-fold crossvalidation yielded an AUC of 0.727 for the clinical model and 0.911 after CML was added.

Thus, the lower serum CML signal was not readily explained by the measured demographic, renal, or metabolic differences and provided substantial additional discriminatory information beyond the selected clinical variables.

Nevertheless, these results arise from a case-control cohort and still require independent external validation before they can be interpreted as generalizable clinical performance or used to define a diagnostic threshold.

Its potential value is therefore complementary rather than substitutive.

The limitations include the single-cohort, cross-sectional case-control design, which precludes causal inference and longitudinal prediction, as well as absent external validation, residual confounding, and small exploratory analyses.
Neither ELISA fully resolves circulating CML molecular pools or identifies modified proteins.
The full cohort also lacked uniform amyloid PET, tau PET, or cerebrospinal-fluid confirmation, limiting generalization to biomarker-defined AD.
In addition, clinical diagnosis may introduce classification error relative to biological AD criteria, and the direction of any resulting bias is uncertain.

Future studies should validate the association across cohorts and analytical platforms, determine disease specificity, and follow CML trajectories across cognitive aging, mild cognitive impairment, and AD.
Integrating molecularly resolved CML measurements with lipidomics, metabolomics, renal and dietary measures, intestinal-barrier biology, and microbiome profiles could clarify its biological origins.
Prospective studies should test incremental information beyond established blood biomarkers and associations with progression or treatment response.
Such studies should prespecify analytical targets and normalization procedures to avoid conflating free CML with protein-bound immunoreactivity.
